9et001-jun25-06:
King Lear
The question asked about the presentation of social order.
This proved an effective and accessible question. Most candidates were able to comment on the presentation of social order in terms of society’s failings and its breakdown. Weaker responses tended to describe changes in the social order of the play and how it changed, while stronger responses identified ways in which this challenged or related to Jacobean hegemonic structures.
Some responses interestingly explored key contexts such as ‘the great chain of being’. Stronger candidates incorporated such ideas into detailed discussion of how, by giving up the crown, Lear breaks a key element of the social contract, leading both to his own ‘punishment’ and to the outbreak of civil unrest. Lower level candidates sometimes allowed such contexts to ‘run away’ with responses rather than focusing on their contribution to readings of the play.
There was a tendency, in less effective responses, to include (sometimes lengthy) narrative passages, loosely related to assertions about social systems, power and unrest. Stronger responses incorporated targeted textual reference seamlessly within argument. One examiner was impressed by scripts that suggested Lear ‘brought about his own downfall by going against patriarchal ideals when he encouraged his daughters to speak’, thus setting off a chain of events that further destabilise the world of the play.
Key contextual factors explored included the difference between the newly emergent middle class of Shakespeare’s time and old-blood aristocracy, social constructions of monarchy, social rights and responsibilities and legal status. Some candidates also considered ideas of gender and social status, as well as genre contexts related to the role of social outsiders, such as Edmund and
The Fool.
Integrating coverage of the Assessment Objectives is a skill and a key feature of responses awarded marks in the higher levels.
In this example, we see a candidate discriminatingly weaving contextual and critical ideas into their discussion of the text and the ways in which it deals with concepts related to social order.
Use of settings and symbolism can be a useful way of addressing AO2. For this question, the storm as a symbol of the breakdown of social order and the use of the map in the opening scene as a symbol for the division of Lear’s kingdom are both significant in relation to social and familial breakdown in the play.
9et001-jun25-07:
Othello
The question asked about the extent to which Othello is a flawed hero.
This was the less popular option for Othello, but many thoughtful responses were seen. It encouraged approaches via genre context, and many candidates rose to this challenge. As well as the Aristotelian model of tragedy, many candidates considered how inherent misogyny, racism and social constructions of honour and reputation could define Othello as a flawed hero. A number of stronger candidates engaged thoughtfully with Leavis’ views on Othello’s propensity for ‘self-dramatisation’.
Lower-level responses tended to catalogue features of tragic heroes or to see Othello as unproblematically flawed from the outset on the basis of his race and/or his masculinity.
Some responses considered Othello in relation to other characters – primarily Iago, Desdemona and Cassio – exploring their roles in his downfall. There was some interesting AO2 focus on the play’s shift in locus from Venice to Cyprus and their roles as liminal spaces in shaping Othello’s fate. There was some very effective use of stage and screen performances of the play and the interpretations they offer of Shakespeare’s text.
The task naturally focused on literary context, and examiners commented on some impressive analyses of Shakespeare’s conformity to, and subversion of, Aristotelian and Senecan tragic conventions. Some candidates enriched their argument by considering Nietzschean perspectives on classical tragedy. Others explored literary parallels and divergences between Cinthio’s original and Shakespeare’s version and the effects might have on audiences views of Othello.
In terms of AO2, many candidates noted Shakespeare’s use of dramatic verse and its role in shaping our views of Othello. Others observed Shakespeare’s significant pairing of characters and his use of set pieces such as the handkerchief scene and Iago and Othello’s observation of Cassio.
In this extract we see a candidate offering a clear and relevant response to the task.
The response includes critical ideas, and these are applied in a relevant way to the proposition of the question and to the candidate’s arguments, but these ideas are not developed. Expression is clear throughout. There is some textual reference, though this is localised and not analysed in detail.
Regular close reference to the text is important in making sure that responses are closely related to the play.
The strongest candidates use their critical reading in integrated and evaluative ways in their analysis of the plays. This is well exemplified in the following extract from a Level 5 response.
This candidate draws on a range of readings of Othello and demonstrates a very clear understanding of how the characters and events of the play might be interpreted in different ways. They draw freely on these critical interpretations in developing their own informed personal response to the play.
9et001-jun25-08:
Othello
The question asked about the presentation of manipulation.
This proved to be the more popular question on Othello. On the whole, candidates engaged well with the task. Almost all candidates dealt, at least in part, with the theme of manipulation by considering the character of Iago, and many candidates dealt with him exclusively. This was a perfectly valid approach to the task, and was handled very well by many.
Many commented on issues such as the basis of his skilful manipulation of others in both his psychological insight into those he despises and in his linguistic felicity. The latter was examined in detail through consideration of Shakespeare’s use of deliberately audible asides, imagery, insinuation, echoing, rhetorical questions, false but credible and eloquent assertions of love and loyalty. There were, however, less effective examples, in which responses drifted into being a less focused character analysis of Iago. Some candidates also considered other examples of manipulation in the play. Examples include Othello’s manipulation of the Senate, Desdemona’s efforts to manipulate her husband in lobbying for Cassio, and Othello’s final speech in an attempt to manipulate posterity.
Lower-level responses tended to rely heavily on Coleridge’s assertion of Iago’s ‘motiveless malignity’ with little consideration of what this might mean and how it shapes understanding of the play. Stronger answers engaged in a range of ways with whether Coleridge is correct in his views, thinking about a variety of potential motivations for Iago’s manipulative behaviour, including racial prejudice, and sexual and/or professional jealousy. There was also much discussion of the ways in which manipulation is tempered by the play’s repeated assertion that
Iago is ‘honest’. Some responses took this further by exploring how male characters manipulate the identities of women, or how Iago also manipulates the audience, suggesting that he weaponises the racial prejudices of a Jacobean audience to create a first impression of Othello, before he enters the stage.
A wealth of contextual and critical material was seen. Answers made good use of writings by Leo
Africanus, Elizabeth I’s expulsion of black people from England, and a number of candidates used the character of Aaron from Titus Andronicus as a comparative literary context. Some included reference to various staged or adapted versions of the play. AO5 was often addressed effectively, many candidates demonstrating the ability to apply purposefully critical concepts derived from – amongst others – Loomba and Honigman.

9et001-jun25-09:
A Midsummer Night’s Dream
The question asked about the play’s use of contrast.
This question elicited a wealth of interesting ideas from candidates at a variety of levels. Many responses drew on the play’s many straightforward contrasts and divides: between, for instance,
Athens and the forest, male and female characters, human and fairy realms, waking and dreaming, higher- and lower-class characters, or between different generations. More discriminating and sophisticated responses also considered a range of the play’s many conceptual contrasts, discussing issues such as the contrasts between liberty and imprisonment, between illusion and reality, between individual and society, between free will and constraint, between love and hatred. Such discussions generated some very thoughtful ideas. Many candidates were able to place their arguments within a broader consideration of Shakespearean comedy and its tropes, including the ways in which the play often comes perilously close to tragedy.
There was some very good consideration of AO2 – though this was not always addressed – considering a variety of Shakespeare’s methods, including his use of rhymed and unrhymed verse, the dramatic function of Pyramus and Thisbe, the pairing and contrasting of characters, use of contrasting settings.
Contextual and critical ideas were often relevantly and clearly used, many candidates drawing on social-, political- and gender-based contexts and concepts. Many also made use of literary contexts, drawing on other examples of Shakespearean comedy, as well as Romeo and Juliet. In some responses these references appeared mainly as information, but in other cases they were developed in informative and fruitful ways. References to the almost ubiquitous ‘green world’ were often less effective, as candidates tended to leave this phrase to speak for itself without either referencing its provenance in the work of Northrop Frye or explaining how and why this is a valuable concept.

A Midsummer Night’s Dream
The question asked about the presentation of the four young lovers.
This was the less popular of the two questions on A Midsummer Night’s Dream. Many candidates explored in detail the ‘ins and outs’ of the shifting relationships between the characters. In the case of less effective responses, this tended to be rather narrative and descriptive, while more able candidates were able to explore how the twists and turns of the plot illustrate the fragility and vulnerability of the characters concerned. There was also some useful discussion of the ways in which these events are experienced differently by the male and female characters. Surprisingly few responses commented on the ways in which Shakespeare’s presentation of the young lovers leads to confusion – for the characters in the play and for audiences alike. Several candidates considered especially carefully the character of Hermia and her presentation in the opening scene of the play, where we see her placed in relief against an array of significant male characters. Other common issues for exploration included a comparison of the young lovers to the older lovers in the play – Theseus and Hippolyta, Oberon and Titania – and to the
Mechanicals.
As with Question 9, not all candidates were effective in addressing AO2. However, useful comments were made on methods such as the use of verse, the final scene with its play-within- the-play, the shifting pairings and alliances of characters, and Shakespeare’s employment of different settings.

Measure for Measure
The question asked about the presentation of the play’s ending.
Candidates across the range were able to identify the troubling ambiguity of the play’s ending and the extent to which it can be considered a comedy. Many engaged with this difficulty by considering the play’s ambiguous use of marriage and exploring whether these marriages represent some kind of restoration and resolution at the end of the drama or whether, instead, they carry their own disturbing overtones that constitute Measure for Measure a ‘problem play’.
The significance of the title of the play and its rooting in biblical notions of justice, punishment and judgement was considered by many candidates, along with some interesting exploration of how this might have been seen differently by Shakespeare’s contemporary audience as compared to audiences today. Another popular focus for discussion was related to the relative outcomes for the male and female characters and the extent to which the play’s ending provides an imbalanced ‘justice’.
Discussion of Shakespeare’s method in employing a trial-like setting for the final scene provided some interesting debate. Some commented on this as a liminal setting ‘near the city gate’, reflecting the final scene’s attempt to bring together the oppositions the play has revealed.
Others considered the significance of the Duke’s use of disguise. Some candidates made use of stage and screen performances of the play, and stronger candidates gave thoughtful consideration to how these interpretations affected their personal responses to the troubling ending of the play.

9et001-jun25-12:
Measure for Measure
The question asked about the presentation of death.
Fewer candidates writing on Measure for Measure opted for this question. Those who did explored the play’s use of death in both literal and figurative terms. It was somewhat surprising that so many, in a play so steeped in death, restricted themselves to using the sentence on Claudio as a springboard for discussion of Angelo’s hypocrisy. Few mentioned the Duke’s 'Be absolute for death…' or Claudio’s 'Ay, but to die…', which are key markers in the play’s consideration of death and mortality. There was also little reference made to Barnardine and his stolid refusal to die.
Candidates offered insight into a range of interesting ways in which the idea of death can be figuratively applied to the events of the play. There was, amongst others, consideration of the death of justice and honesty in the Viennese court, the death of honour and the death of social cohesion.
Many responses engaged in discussion of the play’s genre. They observed its designation as a comedy in the First Folio, going on to question the extent to which the play flirts with tragedy (and death) and is to be seen as a ‘problem play’. Several considered the play in relation to the political world of Shakespeare’s day, exploring notions of statesmanship and social order. Others discussed Shakespeare’s use of Cinthio’s story of Epitia from Hecatommithi, a similar tale that ends in tragedy and Whetstone’s drama Promos and Cassandra, which includes more comic elements.

The question asked about the extent to which the play is a dark comedy.

9et001-jun25-14:
The Taming of the Shrew
The question asked about the play’s use of irony.
Several candidates worked with the suggestion that Shakespeare is using the content of the play ironically to challenge societal norms and the gendered nature of Elizabethan society. For example, they considered the transformation of Bianca at the end of the play and the extent to which she and other female characters indulge in subversive behaviours. Others suggested that although ostensibly ‘tamed’, there is in fact little change in Kate’s behaviour in the course of the play.
Examiners saw effective engagement with the question of how comedy functions as a genre and the extent to which The Taming of the Shrew and its troubling content can be (or should be) considered comic. Several candidates also commented on the relationship between the play’s Induction and the main drama, considering the ways in which it is important in establishing the ironies of the play.

9et001-jun25-15:
Twelfth Night
The question asked about the presentation of deception.
The theme of deception proved accessible to a wide range of candidates. Most were able to connect this effectively to various dimensions of the play’s plot and many also connected it to
Shakespeare’s dramatic methods. Less effective responses tended simply to identify moments of deception without deeper analysis of the significance or presentation of such moments in the play. Others, however, offered more fully-fledged responses. Typical, in this respect, was the widespread discussion of Shakespeare’s use of disguise and costume in the play, with some candidates offering discriminating analysis of Viola’s cross-dressing as Cesario. This was often connected to gender roles within Jacobean England, the idea of the Carnivalesque, and theatrical practices of male players in the age of Shakespeare. Another popular focus for discussion was the gulling of Malvolio, a topic on which candidates proved able to make purposeful connections to the mocking of Puritanism and Malvolio’s desire for social advancement. This also led to some debate surrounding the morality of deception and deceit. Some candidates also considered the extent to which characters engage in self-deception, such as the Duke’s self-deceptive and self- indulgent views of love or Malvolio’s belief in his own importance.
There was a trend amongst some candidates to use the Viola/Cesario deception plot to suggest that Shakespeare was making statements about gender fluidity. The discussion of reception contexts is, of course, important, but candidates should be aware of the potential difficulties of such attempts to ascribe more modern intentions and perspectives retrospectively. Careful thought and phrasing is required when adopting and pursuing such arguments.
There was some useful discussion of Shakespeare’s use of comedy, observing the prevalence of deception and disguise within the genre, but also observing how near these devices come to making the play a very dark comedy.
Detailed consideration of Shakespeare’s methods was often a weaker element of candidate responses. Here, by contrast, we see a strong example.

9et001-jun25-16:
Twelfth Night
The question asked about the use of different types of comedy in the play.
The genre-based focus of this question led candidates to explore a variety of issues related to the tropes and conventions of comedy. Less effective answers, one examiner observed, ‘struggled to comment on different ‘types’ of comedy – too descriptive in approach.’More effective responses, however, provided controlled and well-informed discussion of the tropes of festive comedy, connecting this out effectively to varied critical perspectives. Some candidates considered how dark some of Shakespeare’s use of comedy is in this play, offering, for example, some confident and purposeful analysis of the baiting of Malvolio as a satirical response to Puritanism
Other areas of coverage included Shakespeare’s use of physical, verbal and visual comedy, the comic effects of deception and gender reversal. Some wrote about how comedy was created through the suffering of others, particularly Malvolio (which was compared to the cruel sports of
Shakespeare’s time, such as bear baiting). Others discussed the ending of the play and the ways in which it moves to typical comic resolution. Some candidates did a good job of developing meaningful comparison between contemporary and modern audiences and how their views of the events of the play might differ, but in some cases such discussions tended to result in gross generalisations that were not so helpful. The role of Feste in the play was considered by many candidates, including analysis of his (and other characters’) humorous wordplay and outrageous behaviour.
The best essays dealt with a range of types of comedy, including farce, slapstick, and the thematic and structural value of comedy, including the cultural significance and traditions of Twelfth Night and comedy as an antidote to hypocrisy and pomposity.

Les Blancs
The question asked about the presentation of Eric.
This was the more popular of the questions offered on Les Blancs. Candidates at all levels were able to approach Hansberry’s presentation of Eric. Less able candidates tended to offer a series of simple observations about his character and his role in the play. More developed responses, however, were able to consider how he is representative of broader complexities and issues at play in the drama. Useful discussion was seen in relation to the legacies of colonialism and the complexities of Eric’s position as a man of mixed race. Many candidates were effectively prepared to discuss Eric’s violent conception as the son of Major Rice and Aquah and how he therefore represents in many ways the figurative ‘rape’ of Ztembe.
There was much well-informed discussion of Hansberry’s dramatic methods, and especially the stage direction in which Eric is first introduced and the ways in which it delineates his liminal role.
Others explored the ways in which he might be fruitfully compared to his brothers, Tshembe and
Abioseh. There was some especially effective comparison with Tshembe – who is an equally but differently conflicted character. Other fruitful discussion was directed at Eric’s role in the play’s final showdown.
Contextual issues were effectively dealt with by many candidates, who were well aware of – and able in many cases effectively to apply – the significance of the play in relation to the American
Civil Rights movement, the politics of African independence, and literary contexts (primarily
Genet’s Les Nègres), but also including other significant postcolonial works by Hansberry and others.
Here is an extract from a Level 3 response.
We see here a candidate responding clearly to some different ways in which the character of
Eric is presented, including how he is seen by other characters. The discussion also builds in some clear and interesting reflection on contexts.

Les Blancs
The question asked about the use of stagecraft.
Fewer candidates opted for this task. However, its focus on Hansberry’s stagecraft in the play meant that many candidates developed a much more concentrated and effective focus on AO2. It was pleasing to see that many of the responses to this question demonstrated candidates’ abilities to connect the dramatic methods the playwright employs to the thematic concerns of the play, its contexts and its plot.
Candidates appeared well-prepared to answer this question and could write in detail about
Hansberry’s use of staging, sound and costume in the play. Detailed consideration was given, for example, to stage directions indicating how characters are attired and why this might be significant and to the different ways in which Hansberry employs sounds for dramatic effect.

Many candidates, as for Question 17, made confident links between the text and its contexts, in particular Hansberry’s experience as an emerging black writer in 1960s USA and her complex relationship with the Civil Rights movement.

9et001-jun25-19:
Doctor Faustus
The question asked about the presentation of learning.
Some good answers were seen to this question, especially when candidates connected the presentation of learning to relevant ideas about knowledge in the Renaissance world. Some strong responses used the idea of learning to provide detailed insights into Marlowe’s presentation of Faustus’ character and his naivety. There were responses at all levels which tended to miss opportunities to discuss the text as drama, many candidates limiting AO2 analysis to Marlowe’s use of language and verse. This is, of course, a significant element of the play, but it is important also to engage with a variety of Marlowe’s other methods. A useful example here is the Chorus’ opening invocation of the Icarus myth. Weaker responses identified the literary allusion but did not go on to analyse its significance in relation to concepts of ambition and learning in the drama. More discriminating responses focused on Icarus as an idealised figure and how he relates both to the character of Faustus and to broader contexts of Renaissance
Humanism.
Where candidates were discriminating and, indeed, evaluative and critical with AO3, they explored how Marlowe uses elements of both of the Renaissance stage and the Morality play form to dramatise the tensions between the Medieval notion of ‘The Great Chain of Being’ and
Renaissance Humanism, linking learning and knowledge to social elevation and the fragility of the
Feudal system at the close of the 16th Century. There was a tendency, however, for some responses to lose themselves in contextual material that, while undeniably interesting and relevant, needs to be carefully applied to the text and the topic under consideration.
Here is a clear and straightforward example of a Level 3 response.
The candidate offers clear and relevant ideas in relation to all three Assessment Objectives.
9et001-jun25-20:
Doctor Faustus
The question asked about the extent to which evil characters are made to appear attractive.
There was a tendency for lower-level responses to this question to conduct a series of short character studies rather than to offer more developed and controlled approaches based on the idea of the attractiveness of evil. Such answers also tended to provide examples of characters who appeared attractive to Faustus but often omitted the ‘evil’ aspect, or treated all the attractive characters as if they were evil (e.g. Helen of Troy).
Stronger responses managed this more effectively and many engaged with how Marlowe’s presentation of evil characters connects to the traditions of the medieval morality play. Good work was on display in relation to the masque of the Seven Deadly Sins, and the playwright’s symbolic use of Helen of Troy, the Old Man, and the Good and Bad Angels. Candidates also discussed Mephistopheles’ pleasing appearance to fool and seduce Faustus as compared to his
‘horrible’ true form, thus revealing the potentially seductive nature of evil. Several candidates, however, also considered the ways in which the attractiveness of evil was also undermined in the play which helped them to develop a nuanced argument.
Some observed how Faustus is blinded by evil characters because of their attractive appearance and what he believes they can offer him, and others wrote of religion and how Marlowe might be warning the audience not to stray from God’s teachings. Some very strong answers also wrote of
Faustus himself appearing attractive to the audience but ultimately falling to evil due to his desires.
The following extract is taken from a borderline Level 4/Level 5 script.
This is the introductory paragraph. Notice how it discriminatingly focuses on the idea of the presentation of evil in the play and how this connects to relevant contexts, including the ways in which audiences might receive and respond to the drama.
Incorporating well-placed initial observations about contexts and methods and connecting these to proposed lines of argument can enhance the effectiveness of introductions.
9et001-jun25-21:
The Duchess of Malfi
The question asked about the extent to which the play is designed to terrify the audience.
The use of terror in the play proved an engaging theme for candidates who selected this question. Weaker responses tended to catalogue scenes in which Webster creates terror in his audience without exploring how such terror is created and how this connects to the contemporary world of the playwright or to other contextualising factors. More effective answers engaged very effectively with a variety of the methods Webster employs in creating an increasing sense of terror and threat as the play develops. Some commented on the role of physical light and darkness and associated imagery, connecting this in some cases to the realities of theatrical performance in Webster’s time. Others observed the steady escalation of mental and physical threat as the play progresses and the accumulation of terror this leads to. There was also some useful comment seen on the effects of isolation of different kinds in the play, Webster’s artful development of trains of imagery, his ability to shock his audience, with action derived from the explicitness of his stage directions, and the impact of the Duchess’ behaviour as a threat to male hegemony.
Here is an extract from a Level 5 answer.
The best answers are usually marked by sophisticated written expression and the fluent incorporation of textual evidence. Note these traits in the example.
9et001-jun25-22:
The Duchess of Malfi
The question asked about the presentation of women in the play.
There were some good answers on this question. Candidates seemed to enjoy discussing the women in the play. Most answers concentrated on the Duchess, but there were some that included Julia and Cariola. Patriarchal power was a dominant issue in responses to this question across all levels. Stronger responses, however, did not simply assert this, offering instead an exploration of some of the nuances in the Duchess’ presentation as both a threat to and vulnerable to patriarchal power. Many candidates selected to write about the role of the brothers in the play. Clear and stronger responses often did this effectively, but in some cases discussion tended to drift into analysis of the men and lost focus on how this related to the presentation of women.
Many answers considered the Duchess and her unusual position in the court at that time and how this places her in a uniquely dangerous position. Some candidates interestingly compared her to Lady Macbeth as a powerful woman who is perceived as a threat.There was some controlled and nuanced analysis of the Duchess’ role, the extent to which she challenges patriarchal control, and male anxieties about female autonomy There was an interesting range of opinion on the Duchess and her part in her own demise.
Candidates wrote of the expected role of women in society, some linking this to ideas of dramatic tragedy and how the Duchess’ attempts to subvert this and carve out her own destiny can only ultimately lead to her downfall and death as well as those around her. The abuse of women by male characters was discussed as well as Webster’s possible views about power and monarchy.
This extract come from a response demonstrating Level 2 characteristics.
Typical of Level 2 is the general description and application of contextual material. This extract includes contextual information, but does not really make it relevant to the issues under discussion.
Try to avoid presenting contextual material just as 'sidebar' information. Always try to connect it to arguments about the text and the topic under discussion.
9et001-jun25-23:
The Importance of Being Earnest
The question asked about the play’s use of uncertainty.
Uncertainty proved a clear and interesting theme for consideration and candidates approached the idea in a variety of ways. Some chose to explore uncertainty in relation to a set of opposing certainties in the play. Many focused on the play’s central focus on the name of ‘Ernest’, what the name represents and the play’s conjuring with the concept of personal origin and identity. Who – if anyone – is Ernest/earnest? This led to, in some cases, well-developed exploration of the idea of certainty and uncertainty in relation to personal identity in the play. Other typical issues for discussion included Wilde’s comic exploration of the relationships between men and women in the play, and who is in control, thus challenging a range of the apparent ‘certainties’ of the
Victorian social order. Naturally, many candidates were intrigued by Wilde’s own highly irregular status in the Victorian scene and the way that his life in many ways captures the uncertainties of the era. Discussion of this was not always effectively applied and controlled, however.
Some candidates wrote well about Wilde’s use of stagecraft, commenting on the role of certain stage directions, his use of dramatic set pieces, food and music to create moments of certainty/uncertainty. Here was much discussion of Bunbury and 'Bunburying' and Wilde’s creation of deliberate creation of uncertainty in the play, as well as the impact of his language use and epigrammatic wit to create a brilliant surface that conceals deeper insecurities and uncertainties both in the play and in late Victorian society.
A characteristic of stronger responses is their embedding of discussion of playwrights' methods and an explanation of the effects thus achieved.
Here the candidate incorporates a discussion of Wilde’s use of diaries and other documents within the play, relating this explicitly to the creation of uncertainty.
9et001-jun25-24:
The Importance of Being Earnest
The question asked about the extent to which the play challenges traditional values.
The question’s focus on challenges to traditional values question encouraged many candidates to engage at length with the contexts for the play. Lower-level responses tended to offer lists of the different occasions in the play where traditional social values are challenged. Stronger responses linked Wilde’s use of characterisation to attitudes towards marriage (e.g. Jack and Cecily’s, or
Algernon’s views), or Lady Bracknell’s obsession with social status. Others explored Jack and
Algernon’s use of fictional identities to escape social obligations and pursue their desires, highlighting the artificiality of Victorian social structures. Distinctions were also drawn surrounding Wilde’s use of younger and older characters in the play and how they might represent shifting social expectations. Many responses demonstrated good contextual knowledge of the text and the ways in which its themes of duality and hypocrisy offer a comedic reflection on the often all-too-serious concerns of the late Victorian era. Stronger candidates were alive to nuances and subtleties in this respect, but weaker candidates tended to offer rather sweeping generalisations about Victorian society. Needless to say, there was widespread discussion of
Wilde’s personally scandalous life and the challenges this posed to traditional values.
The ability of candidates to handle context on Victorian values with control and nuance was usually the key factor which marked out more successful answers to this question.
Level 3 answers are clear and relevant, though ideas are not always developed. Look for these qualities in the following extract.
See here how the candidate includes a number of issues, textual evidence and contextual material relevant to the play’s challenging of social convention. Together these provide evidence of a clear, if not fully developed, response.
9et001-jun25-25:
The Rover
The question asked about the extent to which this is a play about material gain.
Material gain proved an interesting theme for candidates. Weaker answers catalogued situations related to money and other financial issues in the play without really engaging with the ways in which these are presented and their broader significance. Other, stronger responses were able to explore themes such as the notion of the impoverished and exiled Cavaliers, the commodification of women in the play, and the role of women who had no independent wealth and were therefore at the mercy of patriarchal family members. Particularly popular were the discussion of
Angellica Bianca as a financially independent woman and the gulling of Blunt by Lucetta.
Some stronger answers took the opportunity offered by the question to consider how the play might also be about other things and reflect wider concerns. Typical issues included the relationship between the sexes, ideas of personal autonomy and ideas of pleasure and pain. As necessary, better candidates were able to build connections between these issues and the question’s focus on material gain.
Candidates also often wrote well about the contexts in which the play was written and received.
Many were interested in Behn’s highly unusual position as a female professional writer and how this related to issues of female characters’ relationship with finances and financial gain in the play. Many also used Bakhtin’s concept of Carnival as a key context for considering an array of characters and situations in the play in relation to notions of social construction and wealth.
Where questions ask candidates to consider 'the extent to which' a proposition is true of the play, they are free to introduce alternative ideas of their own, provided they always bring this back to the proposition of the question. The candidate in the following extract does this very effectively.
The candidate engages in sophisticated ways with the women of the play, questioning the extent to which their motivations relate to material gain.
Making regular explicit reference to the terms of the question helps candidates to ensure they remain relevant throughout their responses.

The Rover
The question asked about the use of settings in the play.
There was widespread consideration here of Behn’s use of the exotic setting of Naples and the
Carnival setting for the play. Candidates were keen to explore the many opportunities this offers for comedy and deception and for the challenging of social norms and expectations. Many were also aware of the extent to which the Carnival setting is used to expose the threats and dangers the characters face. There was interesting discussion, by stronger candidates, of the significance of Behn’s dramatic use of masks and disguise as methods both of deception and of taking control. This was connected to the use of disguise as well (e.g. Hellena’s dressing as a gypsy and as a man) and the opportunities this provides for concealment and for freedom. Stronger candidates were able to draw on contextualising critical ideas from the work of Bakhtin, some applying these very effectively to the characters and the events of the play. There was also useful discussion of Behn’s use of private and public settings and the range of effects she achieves from these, such as Angellica Bianca’s house or Lucetta’s chamber.
The question’s focus on the play’s use of settings encouraged many candidates to approach AO2 in more detail.

9et001-jun25-27:
A Streetcar Named Desire
The question asked about the extent to which the play makes use of the conventions of tragedy.
This question led to a wide range of responses. Some candidates did not really engage with
‘conventions of tragedy’, and weaker responses tended to write about generalised concepts linked to death and suffering or approached the play by running through a mental ‘ticksheet’ of tragic conventions, rather than considering the extent to which the play is a tragedy. Many candidates in the mid- to higher-range suggested how Williams subverts notions of tragedy by having Blanche metaphorically rather than literally die. More discriminating and evaluative responses established the argument that Williams was influenced by – amongst others –
Aristotle, Seneca, Nietzsche and Miller, but ultimately wanted to create a unique tragedy specific to post-World War Two USA.
There was much useful and well-handled discussion of plastic theatre and expressionism and the ways in which Williams’ use of these provides a particular inflection on the presentation of tragedy. As always, there was considerable focus on Blanche and Stanley, but answers in the mid and upper levels made reference to the roles of Stella, Mitch and Allan Grey and the ways in which they experience personal tragedies of differing kinds.
AO3 was often effectively covered. Candidates frequently grasped the power dynamic between
Blanche and Stanley and what that can also be seen to represent in terms of changes in the southern USA – though this is frequently rather simplistically seen as a dichotomy between ‘old’ (feudal and genteel) and ‘new' (industrial and brutish) South. At the lower end of the mark scheme, candidates tended to rely heavily on Williams’s life as context (alcohol addiction, homosexuality, his sister Rose) without linking these clearly to the text. It is notable, too, that there is still a tendency to suggest that events take place just after the American Civil War rather than in the 1940s.
Good Level 3 responses typically bring together effective textual examples with the consideration of dramatic methods and suitable contexts. Here is an example.
This candidate does not always develop arguments, but they do a good job of bringing together their discussion of the presentation of Blanch and ideas of tragedy. There is some interesting connection of Williams' methods in presenting Blanche and Arthur Miller’s famous views on tragedy.
9et001-jun25-28:
A Streetcar Named Desire
The question asked about the presentation of insecurity.
This was by some margin the more popular question on A Streetcar Named Desire. Many candidates engaged with the idea of insecurity well, but in a significant number of cases, responses tended to become character studies of Blanche and/or Stanley rather than retaining a tight focus on insecurity. It was pleasing to note, however, that there was also much discussion of other characters who experience insecurities of different kinds, such as Stella, Mitch, Allan Grey and Eunice. Some also considered effectively how contextual factors are used to explore broader societal insecurities.
Prompted by Williams’ almost novelistic stage directions, many candidates were able to engage with Williams’ use of stagecraft and the practices of plastic theatre to present insecurity. In less effective answers, candidates often identified that insecurity is presented by devices such as costume, sound, lighting and music. More effective answers were able to engage with how
Williams uses these to suggest the characters’ insecurities and/or the inherent precarity of the situations, people and places they encounter (e.g. Blanche’s feelings of inadequacy and fear of aging or losing status).
Many candidates made good use of context in relation to ideas of insecurity. In lower-level responses, such references tended to be vague (e.g. to Blanche as representative of the Old
South, unable to conform to post-war USA, and Stanley as the representative of the New South).
Stronger answers were able to consider how both of these versions of the South come with their own insecurities – often gender- and class-based. Such answers also often explored how characters behaviours reflected their insecurities (e.g. Stanley’s violence, Blanche’s bathing).
Level 2 responses tend to be general in nature and are often underdeveloped.
In this example, the Assessment Objectives are all covered, but in general and under- developed ways.

Sweat
The question asked about the relationship between Chris and Jason.
This question prompted a range of responses. Some candidates engaged in a full and balanced consideration of the personal relationship between Chris and Jason and how this changes as the drama develops, placing this in the context of the significant social and cultural factors affecting the kind of US community depicted in the play. Other, less effective responses were somewhat perfunctory and only made passing generalised comments on rustbelt crash-era USA. Stronger candidates were also able to discuss in detail the ways in which changing contexts of US racial politics is significant in framing and shaping the relationship between Chris and Jason. Stronger candidates were able to comment on some of Nottage’s dramatic methods, including the role of the dual timeframe of the play, her use of overlapping dialogue and her use of press headlines.

The question asked about the impact of the play’s final scene.
Many candidates observed the significant shift in tone in the final scene of the play, considering how this related back to the event of the rest of the play. 9et001-jun25-31:
Waiting for Godot
The question asked about the presentation of human endurance.
Answers across the full range were seen on this play. Many candidates seemed to approach the play via ‘isms’ – absurdism, existentialism, nihilism and others. Strong candidates proved well- informed on these topics and were able to use them effectively as context and, indeed, as a starting point for the consideration of the playwright’s methods. In the case of lower-level responses, however, these were not always well understood, and this in turn meant that they are not always effectively connected to the play. More effective mid-level responses tended to start by considering the ways in which Beckett explores ideas of human endurance and how audiences might respond to this. Is it disturbing? Is it entertaining? Is it funny? Is it poignant? Does it speak to me? Such issues provide a useful way into considering how contextual background cultural references then feed into personal response. Some also observed – with or without irony – that there are many ways in which the play also pushes audiences to the ends of their endurance.
There was much comment on Beckett’s use of the four central characters and the situations they have (repeatedly – though with some variation) to endure, stage directions, repetitious dialogue and dramatic structures, and the possibility of an end to the need for endurance represented by the leaves on the tree in Act Two. There was also sometimes detailed, sometimes very general reference to a range of contexts. Camus’ The Myth of Sisyphus was widely – if not always effectively referenced – as were contexts related to music hall tropes and the filmography of Laurel and
Hardy. In the best responses these were embedded and rich in their contribution; in weaker answers, they tend to appear as information.

9et001-jun25-32:
Waiting for Godot
The question asked about the extent to which the play can be considered a comedy.
This was the less popular option on Beckett’s play. Some candidates engaged well with the troubling question of the play’s genre, drawing on the playwright’s own designation of the play as a tragicomedy. This naturally feeds into the question’s focus on ‘the extent to which’ the play is actually comic. Weaker responses tended to focus on moments of humour in the play – dark as these moments might be. More developed answers were able to identify the tropes of stage comedy and to use examples from the drama to consider Beckett’s use of them. As with Question
31, there was a tendency for some candidates to approach the play from critical perspectives that could dominate rather than liberating arguments.
The play’s methods – including repetition, slapstick humour, its use of absurd situation, and the almost ubiquitous stichomythia – were used as means of approaching Beckett’s methods in relation to comedy. Other answers took the opportunity allowed by the question to consider whether the play is in fact more tragic than comic in its impact and effects.
A variety of useful contexts related not only to the post-war setting of the play, but also to a range of comic contexts, such as music hall and comic duos such as Laurel and Hardy were effectively used by some candidates.
Here is a full Level 2 response, awarded a mark of 7.
This response covers each of the Assessment Objectives, but in brief, general and under- developed fashion.

9et001-nov21-08:
Othello
The question asked about masculinity.
All candidates chose to answer this question on Othello, and it was the most popular on the paper. Generally, candidates appeared to know the text well and could refer to it in detail. Weaker responses struggled to stay with the topic of masculinity, tending to drift off onto character studies of Iago or Othello.
References to critics were made but not always pursued in detail. Loomba and
Coleridge were referred to most often.
Here is one of the more successful responses to the question. A decent argument is developed (although expression is not always clear and there is a mostly sustained focus on the topic of masculinity. Occasionally references to context seem out of place, but a strength is its use of critical arguments to support the candidate’s own. A relative weakness would be the absence of much discussion around the writer’s craft:
The men of Othello are all, to a certain extent, what a modern audience would call ‘manly’. Many are soldiers and known to be ‘valiant’, yet others exert their dominance in other ways, for example, in Brabantio’s case, through fatherhood. It could also be said that this heavily- valued notion of masculinity is a terrifying catalyst for the tragedy to take hold with such a gripping influence over the male inhabitants of Venice, it’s unsurprising that the threat of lost masculinity wreaks havoc.
Othello is particularly susceptible to the negative effects of lost masculinity due to his attempts to fit into Venetian society, despite his
‘thick lips’ and ‘otherness’. Venice was known as a place of wealth, cosmopolitan culture and political stability, as well as being a place where many Christians adopted Christian values to fit in. Ben Olers said that ‘for a Black man to be somewhat noble in the west, he would have to have been neutralised’. This reigns true for Othello, who, as a racial other, he must exert masculine, Venetian values in order to survive.
Othello’s masculinity is called into question from the very start of the play, with Iago telling Brabantio “an old black ram is tupping your white ewe”.
On the Christian Great Chain of Being, animals are below man, especially noble men, so Iago is essentially depicting Othello as less of a man. With Christianity dominating Venice, peoples belief in the correct order of things would no doubt be vital. |it could also be said that when
Brabantio says “thou hast enchanted her”, the allusion to witchcraft is a largely feminine association. The Witchcraft Act of 1563, made it legal to kill witches accused of curses and this led to the death of nearly 3000 women. However, aside from Iago, Othello is also depicted as the
‘’warlike Moor” he wishes to be. Iago sings “a soldier’s a man” and this close tie of war to masculinity is what makes Othello’s fall from grace all the more effective. Iago’s machinations surrounding the manipulations of masculinity present a show of purpose which could perhaps make us forget that Shakespeare is the brains behind it all. The move from
Venice to Cyprus is followed by the removal of external threat- “our wars are done”. The lack of war and violence means that there’s room for Othello to be nothing but a “lascivious Moor”, his one “ocular proof” of masculinity banished. Therefore Othello’s lack of soldier status and hence masculinity gives Iago room to tragically drag Othello down to his rightful place.
Masculinity is, indeed, something Iago harnesses to carry out his scheming. G Salgado references Iago’s short honeyed sentences and questions, such as “Ha! I like not that” calling into question whether
Othello really does have control of his wife. It could be said that Iago intends to improve his own masculinity and that’s why he knows exactly how to drag Othello down. Complaining that “preferment goes by letter and affection”, Iago wants a promotion in order to move up the ranks into nobility. Here, he displays the archetype of the Malcontent, someone upset with the social order of things, who seeks, through sneaky methods, to rectify it. In improving his own masculinity however, he must not only lessen Othello’s, but also “ensnare as great a fly as Cassio”. It is Iago’s fault that Cassio is demoted and it’s this demotion that lets Iago warn Othello to “look to your wife”. Again, military roles and masculinity are closely linked, and the loss of both set the start point for the tragedy to occur.
Masculinity is also lost in the play through the failure to control womanhood. Ania Loomba said that Othello is predisposed to his negative beliefs about women due to his otherness and this reigns true as we see how his insecurity with his own “visage” makes it easier for
Iago to “prove {Othello’s} love a whore”. At the start of the play Othello has a “divine” and outspoken wife, who he allows to “let her speak of me to her father. He clearly believes marriage should be a union and that masculinity and femininity are somewhat equal, as shown by “she loved me for the dangers I had passed, and I loved her tat she did pity them”. However, upon Iago’s warning to “observe her well with Cassio”,
Shakespeare creates the realms for Desdemona to become Lisa
Jardine’s alleged “passive-victim”. Othello’s inability to control womanhood stems from his belief that he has been cuckolded.
Cuckolding was the ultimate insult to a man’s masculinity, as it implied a man could not control his wife, which, considering the fact that a contemporary Jacobean audience wouldn’t think twice about inter- marriage domestic abuse, a man being cuckolded portrays him as weak.
When Othello “strikes Desdemona” we see an attempt to hold on to his masculine power through any means necessary, similar to that of a
Macchiavelli. …

SECTION B: Other Drama
As usual there were differing approaches to this section, with some candidates focusing heavily on the minutiae of the text and others giving an evaluative view but with little specific evidence.
A Streetcar Named Desire was the overwhelming choice of play. The Importance of Being Earnest saw some responses and a further few had studied Dr Faustus or The Duchess of Malfi
Context was generally handled well, and most candidates were able to link their comments to relevant historical and biographical information. Again, as in previous series, the best responses fully addressed the writer’s craft and considered staging in their textual analysis, rather than just looking at language and dialogue.
Finally, it was clear once again in this section that some candidates had struggled with timing and their responses suffered as a consequence of too long spent on the Shakespeare section.

The question asked about the presentation of Malvolio.

9et001-oct20-16:
Twelfth Night
The question asked about love.
The less popular question. Only a few chose to do it and most responses were located around Level 3 with familiar discussion of Shakespeare’s ‘feminist' message about the liberation of females and so on. Stronger responses explored in detail how Shakespeare used his theme to various dramatic ends. Here is an extract from a high level response to the question. Note the sustained engagment with critical argument:
Throughout ‘Twelfth Night’ Shakespeare treats the theme of love as a powerful force that guides the actions of many of the characters. We see differing kinds of love dictating the actions of many different characters, with often one character being motivated by multiple kinds of love. Familial love, foolish romantic love and self-love are the primary ways in which we see Shakespeare explore the theme which, when looked at in the context of archetypes of the time, such as the
Petrarchan lover and the Puritan, can be understood to serve a greater comedic purpose. Thus we see Shakespeare treat the theme of love as a force that guides, not only the characters, but much of the comedy.
The first way we can come to understand how Shakespeare treats the theme of love is the use of familial love. This love and the grief that comes from loss of family is seen to be a primary motivation for both Olivia and Viola. Schalkwyk argues that the two women are ‘conjoined in the mutual depth of their loss’ of both their brothers. Such an idea is evident from our first impressions of both
Page 5 of 8 characters. When we first hear of Olivia, Orsino states that ‘A brother’s dead love, which she would keep fresh / and lasting in her sad remembrance’. The juxtaposition of the ideas of ‘death’ and ‘fresh’ indicates the eternal nature of
Olivia’s love for her brother and suggests that it is unchanged since his death. We are given a similar first impression of Viola, whose second line in the play is “And what should I do in Illyria? My brother he is in Elysium”. The immediate consideration of her brother, especially when contemplating how she should proceed, highlights the closeness of their relationship. Further, both characters being initially presented in the context of the death of their brothers highlights the importance of familial love to them and draws an immediate parallel between them, illustrating Schalkwyk’s point.
Nonetheless, the depth of Olivia’s loss is somewhat undermined when we consider her interaction with Feste. When Feste asks why she is grieving, and she responds that it’s due to her brother’s death, he answers, ‘The more fool, Madonna, to mourn for your brother’s soul being in heaven. Take the fool away gentlemen. The contrast between referring to her both as ‘madonna’ and ‘fool’ highlights Feste’s role in the household as both Olivia’s servant but also as an insight into the ideas of the play. This insight, and Olivia’s acceptance of it, allows us to see that while
Olivia is in mourning, it is perhaps not as great as Orsino believes and reveals that the depth of her grief may not be as great as we first thought. The character of the
Fool was very common in Shakespeare’s plays... usually giving consistent insight into and comment on the play. Thus, this reflects how an audience at the time would have placed great value into the insight of Feste and would understand how the depth of Olivia’s loss may be being exaggerated. This undermines Schalkwyk’s argument, as Viola’s familial love and grief are shown to be motivating forces until the end of the play...
SECTION B: Other Drama
A Streetcar Named Desire was by far the most commonly studied play, with almost three- quarters of candidates answering on it. The Importance of Being Earnest saw some responses and a further few had studied Dr Faustus and The Duchess of Malfi.
Most responses were clear and and showed, in the main, a good understanding of the plays.
Context was addressed, but often comments were generalised and there was often not enough detailed linking between these contexts and the text itself. As has been the case in previous series, this meant that, although links were clear, they often remained at Level 3 for AO3. Students need to be reminded of the need to address context subtly and circumspectly, particularly in A Streetcar Named Desire. Many wrote about the play as if it were merely a re-enactment of the conflict between Old South and New South, with Blanche and Stanley being merely counters ('allegorical representations' as one candidate put it) for socio-economic forces rather than rounded and complex dramatic characters.
Again, as in previous series, the best responses fully addressed the writer’s craft and considered staging in their textual analysis, rather than just looking at language and dialogue. There were some good examples of this in responses to Q24.
Finally, it was clear in this section that some candidates – definitely more than usual - had struggled with timing and their responses suffered as a consequence of too long spent on the
Shakespeare section.

9et002-jun17-childhood-01:
‘Characters responding to difficult circumstances’
Many candidates linked Hard Times with Atonement and did so successfully. The contrasting authorial voices and narrative structures of Dickens and McEwan provoked fruitful discussion. Some candidates had a thorough grasp of postmodernism; others mentioned it but did nothing with it. On a different level, there were productive comparisons of Briony (too much imagination) and Louisa (too little) who were both seen to have suffered from poor parenting. Utilitarianism was held up as a great evil by many students of Dickens but it often seemed that candidates were unsure what it was. Stephen Blackpool’s approach to his difficult circumstances provided some candidates with a rich source of relevant material but discussions of male characters were comparatively rare. A significant number of candidates managed to discuss Atonement without mentioning World War Two, which was disappointing.
Fewer candidates tackled What Maisie Knew or The Color Purple. James is not an easy read, of course, but there were some very sophisticated answers showing a clear understanding of the underlying socio-historical climate. Responses to Walker ranged widely in terms of quality. Candidates often did not move away from very generic comments on racism and
‘the patriarchal society’. The best answers here showed understanding of pantheism, and a detailed understanding of socio-economic and feminist context. Candidates seemed unable to resist reciting the sexually graphic language on the opening page – but this was often gratuitous.

9et002-jun17-childhood-02:
‘Friendship’
Some candidates limited themselves by simply listing examples of friendship in their chosen novels but others took a more selective and discriminating approach, focusing on friendships which were central to the concerns of each author: Louisa and Sissy in
‘Hard Times’, Celie and Shug in ‘The Color Purple’, Maisie and Mrs Wix or Sir Claude. Some candidates usefully considered Briony’s lack of friends and her flawed alliance with Lola.
A number of candidates discussed the relationships between members of the same family (Louisa and Tom, Celie and Nettie) or romantic involvements (Robbie and Cecilia). These were valid but tended to blur the focus a little.

9et002-jun17-colonisation-and-its-afterm:
‘Exploitation’
Huckleberry Finn was a notable absentee for this question but there were some effective discussions using the other texts: Heart of Darkness being linked to either The Lonely
Londoners or A Passage to India. Exploitation was seen as brutal in Conrad but more subtle in Selvon and it was interesting to see how many candidates showed how women were exploited in both texts rather than the focus being solely on race. Narrative voice is central to our understanding of the texts and there were some engaging discussions of whether we should adopt Achebe’s view that Conrad is a racist, or of Forster’s sympathetic portrayal of Indians. A number of very able candidates explored how exploitation dehumanises the exploiters as well as the exploited, especially in Forster and Conrad, and one candidate effectively invoked Nietzsche’s argument that ‘if you gaze into the abyss, the abyss gazes also into you’ with reference to Kurtz.
This response on The Lonely Londoners and Heart of Darkness just tips into level 5 for AOs
1 and 2 and is more secure on AOs 3 and 4.

Examiner Comments
The argument is clear, if highly selective, and relevant references to context are closely woven into it.

‘Unfamiliar environments’
There were some profitable considerations of how Selvon’s West Indians adapted to London, or how few of Forster’s Britons adapted to India. Huck Finn did make an appearance here and there was a particularly thoughtful discussion of how his journey removes him from society and allows him to listen to his own moral conscience. There were some sophisticated responses which considered the natural environments of India (particularly the Marabar Caves) and the Congo and how these mysterious places served to damage the Europeans who came into contact with them.
This response on The Lonely Londoners and Heart of Darkness was awarded a low level 4 mark for AOs 1 and 2 and a low level 3 mark for AOs 3 and 4.
Examiner Comments
Context is addressed in the opening paragraph but does not re-appear. The argument is controlled but its main thrust is not outlined at the start.
9et002-jun17-crime-and-detection-05:
‘Characters who investigate crime’
There were very few answers on the P.D. James – in a way this text stands out as different to the others in that it is the one conventional ‘crime’ novel, and this in itself poses difficulties for candidates looking at it, especially those with little wider experience of the genre.
Discussion of context was very limited, rather ironically since the murder room in the
Dupayne Museum is predicated on the idea that murders reflect the times in which they are committed. Similarly, the Capote with its awkward balance of fact and fiction poses particular challenges which weaker candidates find it difficult to address.
Considerations of the detectives involved were frequently superficial: Dalgliesh has a team and science on his side whereas Robert Audley does not. Some were able to explore how characters such as Audley or Franklin Blake were developed by their creators, however, and those that considered Al Dewey saw him as an everyman who had little of the success that usually comes to fictional detectives but who had the solidity and commitment to persevere.
Narrative voice, and the way that authors are able to direct the reader’s sympathies, is a very rich seam for study but few candidates exploited it.
This is a strong level 5 response.
Examiner Comments
The candidate pursues a sophisticated argument, well supported with evidence, that makes sustained and relevant links between the two texts.
9ET0_02_Q05_2422064_0429_004579477_005.png
A consideration of context, whilst unobtrusive, is present throughout.
9et002-jun17-crime-and-detection-06:
‘A sense of mystery’
Few candidates attempted this and, again, a study of narrative voice and structure could have been productive but was rarely seen. However, some candidates discussed how authors of crime fiction were able to stage manage the ‘slow leaching of information’ which is the staple of the who- how- or why-dunnit.
9et002-jun17-science-and-society-07:
‘Hope’
Superficial answers considered Frankenstein’s hope that he would be successful, the hope for children in Gilead, the hope for rescue in The War of the Worlds. The more successful considered how hope was integral to narrative structure and narrative voice, focusing on
Offred’s memories of the past or Kathy’s search for deferment in Never Let Me Go.
This is a level 5 answer on The Handmaid's Tale and The War of the Worlds.
Examiner Comments
This is a strong, evaluative argument which keeps the writers of the texts in the foreground and makes links continually.
9et002-jun17-science-and-society-08:
‘Criticise human behaviour’
This was by far the most popular question on the paper. Weaker answers focused on characters who behaved badly (Frankenstein, the curate) but the majority looked at the wider issues involved and the ways in which authors directed our responses. There were many broadly feminist readings, especially in discussions of Shelley and Atwood, which adopted the view that male-dominated societies were subjugating or negating the role of women in fiction and in fact. Shelley was often seen as a proto-feminist, mainly due to her mother, whose treatment of women characters was an implicit criticism of male hegemony and Frankenstein’s attempt to remove the need for women altogether. Candidates often quoted Atwood’s statement that there was nothing in her novel that hasn’t already happened and there were frequent references to Reagan’s and Thatcher’s conservatism and policies in various countries which applied birth control. However, these tended to be bolted on to arguments rather than woven into them.
Those who answered on Ishiguro found it more difficult to apply a consideration of context, although there were some thought-provoking explorations of how the powerful manipulated the weak in society. The War of the Worlds featured less prominently but the candidates who had studied Wells were often able to construct some strong arguments about his criticism of Imperialism, his use of the contrasting standpoints taken by the curate and the artilleryman and the triumph of Nature at the end of the novel.
This is a level 3 response on Frankenstein and The Handmaid's Tale.
Examiner Comments
This is a clear response which uses both texts and shows awareness of the writer's craft. The argument tends to explore and describe rather more than it analyses and references to context are not fully integrated.
9et002-jun17-the-supernatural-09:
‘characters who experience anxiety’
It was tempting, here, for candidates to pick out characters who went through difficult times and describe how they reacted to them. Such an approach clearly does not go far enough, however, and more successful answers looked at the very nature and origins of the anxiety experienced. Thus, it was possible to see both Wilde and Stoker using their characters to voice the contextual anxieties about atavism, immigration and vice. Similarly, Waters used characters to demonstrate anxieties about the decay of privilege and the rise of the working class whilst Morrison explored the deep-rooted legacy of slavery. Although the theme of The
Supernatural links all four texts, it is important for candidates to examine what the texts are really about.
This response to The Picture of Dorian Gray and Dracula was awarded marks low in level 4.
Examiner Comments
The response is fully focused on the question and the candidate presents a controlled, structured argument. The elements of the argument are supported by discriminating reference to context and integrated links between the two 19th century texts.
9et002-jun17-the-supernatural-10:
‘Violence’
Again, there were a large number of broadly descriptive responses. Better ones explored how violence was a response to deep-seated contextual concerns such as the worrying sexualisation of women in Dracula or Victorian xenophobia. Some candidates examined the way violence was presented and this sometimes gave rise to detailed word-level analysis which ultimately proved sterile and distracting. There were, however, some very successful responses examining the use to which writers put violence – as catalyst, as catharsis as well as a crime. One particularly thoughtful response discussed how violence could be seen as heroic in Dracula and Beloved. Similarly, violence was sometimes seen as an expression of despair in Wilde and Waters.
This response on The Picture of Dorian Gray and Dracula was awarded marks in level 5.
Examiner Comments
This is a fluent, coherent argument, supported well by some close references to both
9ET0_02_Q10_2250121_0429_004216688_005.png texts and analysis of detail. There is a confident overview of the concerns of each writer in the light of contextual factors, supported by well-chosen, embedded quotations.
9et002-jun17-women-and-society-11:
‘Loss’
In the main, candidates saw the need to interrogate the distinct nature of loss in each text studied. There were many interpretations and lines of argument, considering the loss of ambition, or freedom, or education. There were a good many answers that focused on the loss of identity, particularly when it came to the central characters in Mrs Dalloway or
A Thousand Splendid Suns but also in Wuthering Heights. However, this view often led to formulaic and reductive arguments about the way women are treated in male-dominated societies. Much more productive were the responses which paid proper attention to authorial or narrative voice and there were some particularly perceptive criticisms of the paternalism and manipulative techniques adopted by Hardy. Similarly, some examined
Bronte’s use of a variety of narrators in order to direct reader response.
This response on Mrs Dalloway and Tess of the D'Urbevilles was awarded marks in level 5.
Examiner Comments
Coverage of the texts is sophisticated. The response is fully focused on the question and contextual ideas are embedded. There is evaluation of the writers' use of structure to shape meaning. The tone is confident and there is an interweaving of detail with overview.
9et002-jun17-women-and-society-12:
‘Attempts to find happiness’
Most candidates attempted to define the nature of the happiness sought by women characters but there was a tendency to focus on the obstacles that stood in their way rather than on how they attempted to find it. Again, patriarchy and male domination were the principal culprits but religion, in Hardy and in Hosseini, came under fire, as did social convention in Woolf and Bronte. The better arguments considered the way that narrative voices either empowered or made passive the relevant characters: through Mrs Dalloway’s internal debate, for example, or through the way Bronte and Hosseini range across generations to edge towards some kind of resolution.
The Women and Society theme is understandably popular but candidates should pay close attention to the nature of the texts they study and avoid using them as stepping stones towards sweeping generalisations about how women are treated. Context is best used when it is nuanced, specific and accurate. Otherwise, it can become employed as a specious form of rhetoric, as this candidate colourfully demonstrates: ‘Tess is repeatedly groped by the patriarchal hand of the nineteenth century’.
This response on Wuthering Heights and Tess of the D'Urbevilles was awarded marks high in level 2.
Examiner Comments
The response tends to remain outside the texts.
There is the beginning of a clear argument but there is limited detailed analysis of the writer's craft and references to context are very general.
9et002-jun18-childhood-01:
Many responses to this question focused on the effects of inequalities within society on individual characters. This provided a useful way into the question which the most successful answers were then able to broaden out into a discussion of authorial criticisms of society. Candidates were able to focus on a wide range of aspects of society, including issues surrounding social class, race, gender, sexuality, religion and education, as well as specific historical comments on concerns within
19th and early 20th century Britain.
The focus of the question on society led to contextual factors being considered very successfully, and these comments were often well integrated into the arguments being put forward. Less secure responses tended to list the ways in which society could be criticised, rather than analysing the ways in which writers formulated these criticisms. However, many candidates showed a clear awareness of authorial intent, with some interesting comparisons being made between Dickens’ use of Gradgrind to criticise utilitarianism and McEwan’s use of Emily Tallis to criticise
Chamberlain’s policy of appeasement during the 1930s.
Contextual comments on Atonement tended to be slightly less successful, largely limited to rather vague ideas about class snobbery and prejudice without further development or specific exemplification. There also appeared to be some confusion about the time of writing, with several candidates confusing this with the time setting of the novel and asserting that McEwan was making contemporary comments on 1930s society.
What Maisie Knew was the least popular text, although it was pleasing to see that candidates answering on this novel were able to engage in meaningful discussions of 19th century changes to divorce laws and the moral questions which this raised.
This is the beginning of an essay on The Color Purple and Hard Times which was awarded an overall mark in level 5.
This is a good example of a focused introduction.
The candidate narrows down the question (the ways in which the writers criticise aspects of society) by selecting specific areas to focus on (criticisms of racism, patriarchy and injustice).
There are also brief references to several contextual factors which the candidate returns to in more detail later in the essay. The introduction also begins to make connections between the texts.
If the question you are answering is very broad, use your introduction to narrow it down by outlining what areas you are going to discuss. Your introduction is also a good place to start comparing the texts overall before you start your detailed analysis and comparisons.
This essay on Atonement and Hard Times was given a mark at the bottom of level 5.
This essay is very good at integrating the comments on contexts, comparisons and analysis of the writer's craft. The argument has three distinct strands; the candidate examines the authors' criticisms of children's upbringing, social class structures and gender roles. This makes for a very well structured essay.
A useful way of structuring your essay is to have clear lines of argument in each section.
9et002-jun18-childhood-02:
‘The role of education, formal or informal, in the lives of characters’
The key to success in this question was to consider not only education in the abstract, but the impact it had upon characters, and most answers were able to closely analyse characters in the texts. There were interesting comparisons made between the impact of different styles of education in the novels, such as the very formal, reductionist utilitarian approach in Hard Times, the informal education Celie receives from other women, the ambiguous social and moral education of
Maisie and Briony’s liberal education and need for self-expression in a post-war context. Many responses also considered the lack of education, whether formal or in aspects of personal or social growth. Analysis of writer’s craft varied considerably in responses, from simplistic comments about the repetition of ‘facts!’ in Hard Times to much more in depth consideration of narrative voice.
An effective approach was seen in essays which contrasted Hard Times and Atonement, the former showing the danger of failing to educate and encourage imagination while the latter criticizing unrestrained imagination. The similarity between these texts was also noted as both gaps in education led to the condemning of an innocent man. This was seen as representative of the poor treatment of the working class by the upper classes.
This essay on What Maisie Knew and Atonement was given marks low in level 5.
This essay is very good in AO2. The candidate focuses closely on individual words and the meanings they create, but also considers narrative style and shows their knowledge of the whole text.
In your analysis of the writer's craft, try to balance close analysis of individual words with comments about the overall structure, style and narrative of the whole text.
9et002-jun18-colonisation-and-its-afterm:
‘Attitudes to race’
Very few answers were seen on The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, while Heart of Darkness was very popular, paired with either The Lonely Londoners or A Passage to India. The coverage of AO3 in this theme was well considered compared to last year. The question leant itself to relevant contextual discussion of Belgian Imperialism in the Congo and British colonisation and its legacy, and some candidates drew interesting and thought-provoking parallels with contemporary issues such as the
Windrush scandal. There were interesting comparisons made between modern and contemporary approaches to race with some excellent focus on the changing views on Conrad’s approach. A successful approach was to consider how Conrad and Forster presented European races as well as
African/Indian, for example finding the ‘ugliness’ and ‘savagery’ expected of the Congolese present in European characters, and the exposure of the hypocrisy and injustice of the British in India.
Comparisons between these different contexts were often effective and, in some cases, drew thoughtful conclusions regarding the portrayal of race in literature.
Most answers drew connections between language used in the text and attitudes to race with some thoughtful analysis of the writers’ aims and the presentation of the other. There were a number of strong analyses of Selvon’s craft and the impact of using non-standard English in his characterisation. One candidate commented that the African natives in Heart of Darkness were described as ‘nameless’ and ‘savages’, making them seem ‘inferior and a different species to the
Europeans, making the ability to commit atrocities much easier’. This was a good example of a perceptive comment upon a fairly straightforward example which focuses well on how a writer shapes meaning within a text.
